title: The Kharad Compact
subtitle: From rival trade cities to a league of agreements
summary: Cities that grew rich at the crossings, wars too expensive to win, the Seven Tables, an Assembly that rules by exclusion, and the day the Glass Compass found the silver.
content:
> *"Nothing durable exists without agreement."*
> — Kharadi principle

The **Kharad Compact** is not a country in the way Aurelia is a country. It is a league of wealthy city-states, merchant houses, caravan cities, ports, banking families and trading enclaves, bound together by treaties, shared rules and mutual interest. Foreign maps colour it in a single shade. Kharadis themselves are far more likely to think in terms of **cities**, **houses**, **commercial networks**, **treaty obligations** and **jurisdictions**.

What holds the Compact together is a set of values more than a flag: agreement, reputation, patient negotiation, honest measure, reliable relationships, and value properly understood. Its people are patient, precise and attentive to wording. They want to know what is being promised, who bears the cost, what happens tomorrow, and whether the arrangement is fair enough to last. Foreigners who mistake this for greed tend to come away from the negotiating table poorer and better informed.

This entry covers how the Compact came to be and how it wields power. Its faith is described in [[covenant-of-the-one|The Covenant of the One]], its streets and masks in [[markets-under-painted-glass|Markets Under Painted Glass]], and the darkest chapter of its history in [[silencing-of-the-schools|The Silencing of the Schools]].

## Cities at the Crossings

The Kharadi world grew up wherever movement naturally gathered: at river crossings, along caravan routes, in mountain passes, around harbours, on island ports and in the great inland market towns.

These cities grew rich because they connected other places. Their power never rested on vast territories. It rested on controlling **movement**, **credit**, **exchange**, **storage**, **insurance** and **recognised contracts**. A Kharadi city might hold very little land and still be indispensable to everyone around it.

## The Cost of War

Kharadi political culture was shaped by repeated wars between wealthy commercial cities, and by the lesson those wars taught: *a war can be expensive even when you win*. A victorious city might gain territory and lose its trade, its ships, its creditors, its markets, its partners and years of productive investment.

Over time, competition between the cities shifted toward tariffs, exclusive contracts, finance, monopolies, arbitration and commercial pressure. Violence never vanished. But formal negotiation became more prestigious, and very often more profitable, than fighting.

## The Seven Tables

The turning point came with the **Seven Tables**, one of the foundational legal and commercial traditions of Kharad. They emerged after a period of ruinous trade wars, and set out broad rules for contracts, commercial appeals across city borders, transferable and inherited debt, the protection of merchants, declared tariffs, cooperation against piracy and the recognition of commercial claims.

Their exact wording and the date they were agreed are not settled in any record the Archive holds. Their importance is not in doubt: *they made trade between rival cities predictable enough to continue even while those cities disliked one another*. Kharadis remember the Seven Tables as the moment their world began to become a network instead of a collection of competitors.

> **As the story of the Seven Tables is told in Kharadi schools**
>
> The delegates had been arguing over a single clause since the morning: whether a debt owed to a merchant of one city could be claimed in the courts of another.
>
> "If we allow it," said the delegate from the river city, "your creditors will be in our courts by the end of the season."
>
> "If you don't," said the delegate from the port, "nobody in my city will lend to anybody in yours again. Which, I would point out, is roughly what has been happening for six years."
>
> There was a long silence. Through the window, everyone could see the harbour, with half its berths empty.
>
> "Write it down," said the river delegate at last. "Before I change my mind."

## The Concordat Assembly

The modern Compact is coordinated through the **Concordat Assembly**. It is not a strong central government in the Aurelian sense, and it cannot easily give orders to every member city. What it does well is set standards, recognise agreements, arbitrate disputes, coordinate sanctions, manage shared commercial rules and protect the trade interests the cities have in common.

Its power comes from something quieter than command: exclusion from the network can be economically devastating. A city that ignores every Compact ruling may discover that its letters of credit are no longer honoured, that insurers will not cover its ships, that warehouses deny it access, and that other cities have stopped recognising its contracts. Kharad exercises power through **participation and exclusion** at least as much as through force.

> **The week after a city refused an Assembly ruling, from a factor's letters home**
>
> *Monday. The council declared that the Assembly has no authority here. There were speeches. The square was very pleased with itself.*
>
> *Wednesday. Our insurers have written, very politely, to say they are "reviewing exposure" on all cargo bound for this port.*
>
> *Thursday. Two banks have declined our letters of credit, with apologies. A third has not replied.*
>
> *Saturday. Nobody in the square is making speeches. The council has asked the Assembly, very politely, whether it might be possible to reopen the matter.*

## Houses, Credit and Reputation

**Merchant houses** can be enormous institutions. A house may control or take part in banks, warehouses, shipyards, insurance, caravans, auction houses, intelligence networks, import monopolies and export contracts. Not every house is simply a family. Some are dynasties; others are long-lived commercial institutions that have outlasted any family that founded them.

Kharad treats banking and credit as extensions of trust. A letter of credit lets someone in one city rely on a reputation built in another, and that is what makes long-distance trade, bonded warehouses, transferable debt, great ventures and expedition finance possible. As Kharadis put it, **credit is trust made portable**. This is why fraud is taken so seriously in the Compact: it damages not only one transaction but the network that makes every future transaction possible.

Wealth alone does not earn respect. Kharadis admire **judgment**, **reliability**, sound **risk assessment**, **fair dealing** and the ability to **maintain relationships**. A merchant who wins every negotiation but leaves nobody willing to deal with them again is considered a fool. The ideal deal leaves room for another deal tomorrow.

## Sea Roads

Kharadi cities keep merchant fleets, escorts, private security and, at times, privateers. Their ships favour cargo capacity, range, modular design and defensibility over show. Piracy is tolerated as long as it is merely annoying. When it threatens commerce seriously enough, it becomes a collective problem, and Kharad can respond to it with startling aggression, because by then doing so has become good business.

## Kharad and the Other Powers

- **The [Aurelian Empire](factions.html#aurelian-empire).** Deeply interdependent. Kharad provides finance, insurance and commercial expertise; Aurelia provides vast markets, naval routes and imperial shipping. They disagree regularly and keep profiting from one another.
- **The [Vardic Holds](factions.html#vardic-holds).** Warm, practical relations. Vards appreciate straightforward trade and are suspicious of sophisticated debt and long, complicated obligations. Kharadis tend to find this caution sensible, if a little unsophisticated.
- **The [Vesper Republic](factions.html#vesper-republic).** An important customer and a loud critic. The Republic depends on Kharadi credit, investment and trade, and attacks concentrated wealth, debt and financial power in the same breath. The argument is endless, and both sides seem to enjoy it more than they admit.
- **The [Tianzhao Mandate](factions.html#tianzhao-mandate).** One of the oldest great trade relationships in the world. Both cultures are comfortable with patience, negotiation, long memory and complex protocol. They do not always agree, but neither expects an important negotiation to be quick.
- **[Verna](factions.html#verna).** Distant, complicated and functional, for reasons that go back to [[silencing-of-the-schools|the Silencing of the Schools]].

## What Is This Worth?

Kharad recognised the economic importance of Gate materials immediately. Auctions, speculative markets, salvage claims, expedition finance and insurance appeared almost as soon as the first artifacts came home. The first Kharadi question about anything from beyond a Gate is usually: *what is this worth?*

That is not simple greed. Kharadi thought distinguishes carefully between **value** and **price**. Something can be valuable in ways money expresses badly, and Gate artifacts change hands in Kharad for influence, information, access, favours, political concessions and rights of first refusal as often as for coin. As a Kharadi saying has it, *the Final Measure is not price*.

### The Glass Compass Crash

The Compact's most famous Gate-era lesson about value is the **Glass Compass Crash**. An artifact was rumoured to be able to predict or identify future market conditions. Speculation exploded. Investors convinced themselves the device would give its owners an enormous financial advantage, and a bubble formed around it and everything connected to it.

Then someone worked out what the device actually did. It pointed toward the nearest **refined silver**.

> **On the exchange floor, the day it broke, as one trader remembered**
>
> The Compass had been brought out for a demonstration, and it had been swinging toward the east gallery all morning. Half the floor had already bought into the eastern caravan houses on the strength of it.
>
> I happened to be standing beside it when a cashier from one of the smaller houses walked past on his way to lunch. The needle swung after him like a dog after its master.
>
> He stopped. It stopped. He took two steps to the left. So did the needle.
>
> He looked down at the purse on his belt, very slowly, and then up at the rest of us.
>
> I have never heard a room go so quiet, or empty so fast.

The crash destroyed several major positions. **Three merchant houses collapsed. A fourth made a great deal of money selling silver.** Kharadi economists still argue over whether the Glass Compass "worked". The story is told to every apprentice as a lesson in speculation, in what you do and do not know, and in the danger of pricing something before you understand what it actually does.

## Before the Compact

The modern Compact is not the same thing as every state or dynasty that has ruled Kharadi lands. At one point in the past, an older Kharadi regime became more expansionist, more centralised and more religiously aggressive than the Compact has ever been, and conquered the **Old Scholastic Coast**. What followed is told in [[silencing-of-the-schools|The Silencing of the Schools]], and modern Kharadis disagree, sometimes bitterly, about what they owe for it.
